section_summary: This section documents Japanese military activity and authority in Manchuria and China from 1934 to 1938. It begins with diplomatic correspondence over pressure on foreign firms to finance Dairen’s air defenses, followed by a report on a citywide blackout exercise. Later documents analyze the Kwantung Army’s autonomy, finances, recruitment plans, and relationship with Tokyo, and report rumors of its reorganization; the final telegram concerns military-training films requested by the Kwangtung provincial authorities in Canton.

subfiles.title: Foreign Firms Requested to Contribute towards Air Defense of Dairen
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the Dairen authorities’ solicitation of substantial foreign-business contributions for air-defense maneuvers and equipment.
subfiles.summary: Mayor J. Ogawa’s Air Defense Contribution Committee assigned requested contributions to foreign firms, including ¥3,000 each from two banks and ¥2,000 from Standard-Vacuum Oil. Foreign managers considered the requests excessive and feared commercial retaliation, but most agreed collectively to ignore the letter; Frazer, Federal Incorporated reportedly intended to pay its comparatively small assessment.

subfiles.title: Translated Contribution Request from the Dairen Air Defense Contribution Committee
subfiles.from: J. Ogawa, chairman, Dairen Air Defense Contribution Committee
subfiles.about: Requests a designated contribution toward urban air-defense preparations.
subfiles.summary: The form letter congratulates its recipient on increasing prosperity and states that the committee has assessed an appropriate contribution. Invoking the seriousness of the current crisis and the importance of urban air defense, Ogawa asks the recipient to comply.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 126 Requesting the Status of the Dairen Contributions
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Orders the Embassy to determine the current status of Dairen’s solicitation of foreign firms.
subfiles.summary: The Department refers to Vincent’s June 29 despatch on air-defense contributions. It directs the Embassy to obtain an update from him and report promptly by telegraph.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 74 on Possible Compulsion and Treaty Infringement
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Considers whether fear of retaliation made Dairen’s donation requests incompatible with the 1911 treaty.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy was awaiting evidence about direct or indirect compulsion in the contribution campaign. Grew states that coercive requests might violate Article I of the 1911 treaty with Japan and reports that Vincent was being asked for an immediate update.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 164 on the Second Ogawa Letter
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports a renewed request for donations and asks whether Japan should be approached about possible treaty implications.
subfiles.summary: Vincent reported that American and other foreign firms had received another letter from the mayor as the contribution deadline approached, but none intended to respond and no direct or indirect compulsion had occurred. Grew nevertheless argued that fear of retaliation placed American firms in a position contrary to the spirit of the 1911 treaty. He requested instructions on raising the matter informally with the Japanese Foreign Office.

subfiles.title: Instructions to Protest the Dairen Mayor’s Action
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Directs the Embassy to seek Japanese disavowal of the Dairen mayor’s contribution campaign.
subfiles.summary: The Department instructs the Embassy to speak orally with the Minister for Foreign Affairs, cite Article I of the 1911 treaty, and request measures preventing reprisals against American firms. Vincent was to tell American concerns confidentially to report any suspected retaliation for investigation and prompt transmission to Washington.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 171 Reporting Oral Representations
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports that the Embassy protested the Dairen solicitation and that local anxiety had diminished.
subfiles.summary: Grew states that oral representations were made on August 1 and that a Foreign Office reply was expected. Vincent reported that foreign managers in Dairen no longer viewed the danger of discrimination or retaliation as seriously as they had initially.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 186 Reporting Japanese Disavowal
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the Japanese Government’s rejection of compulsory foreign contributions for Dairen air defense.
subfiles.summary: The Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs informed Grew that the Japanese Government disapproved of the mayor’s action. The Governor of the Kwantung Province had ordered that contributions from foreigners were neither to be exacted nor expected, and the Vice Minister promised that no indirect pressure or retaliation would occur.

subfiles.title: Further Report on Contributions toward Dairen Air Defense
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits the mayor’s renewed letter and identifies the American firms that received it.
subfiles.summary: Vincent explains that Ogawa’s July 20 letter was received by foreign firms shortly before the July 31 closing date and that the committee hoped to raise ¥700,000. The Standard-Vacuum Oil Company and National City Bank of New York were the American recipients, previously assessed at ¥2,000 and ¥3,000 respectively.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference to Grew’s Report on Dairen Contributions
subfiles.from: Department of State records staff
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to another file for Grew’s report on the Dairen mayor’s request.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to file 894.00 P.R./80 for report no. 917 from Japan, dated August 4, 1934. Its subject is the mayor’s request that foreign firms contribute financially toward Dairen’s air defense.

subfiles.title: Request of the Mayor of Dairen that Foreign Firms Contribute Financially toward Air Defense
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State, author not stated
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Dairen contribution controversy and the American treaty-based protest.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that most American firms refused the mayor’s requests but feared commercial retaliation. It quotes the 1911 treaty’s exemptions from compulsory military service, forced loans, and military exactions, then records the Embassy’s request that Japan disavow the mayor and protect American nationals and companies.

subfiles.title: Practice for the Air Defense of Dairen
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Describes a highly effective citywide blackout during a simulated air raid.
subfiles.summary: During celebrations of the thirtieth anniversary of the Russo-Japanese War, Dairen staged the first of two nighttime air-raid exercises. On the signal of approaching enemy aircraft, inhabitants extinguished virtually every visible light for ten minutes. Grummon considered this compliance striking evidence of official discipline and patriotic sentiment; another raid was scheduled for March 11.

subfiles.title: Handwritten Routing Note concerning an FE Copy for MID
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, author not legible
subfiles.about: Suggests lending or forwarding the Far Eastern Affairs copy of a report to Military Intelligence.
subfiles.summary: The fragmentary handwritten note appears to recommend lending FE’s copy to MID. It indicates that the other copies may already have been destroyed, but the underlying report is not identified on the page.

subfiles.title: Request from MID for Mukden Report No. 264
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Records a Military Intelligence Division request to see Mukden’s report no. 264.
subfiles.summary: The note says that Miss Van Lyne of MID telephoned seeking report no. 264 from Mukden, identified there as dated May 12, 1936 and filed under 894C.20/10. It asks whether a copy should be sent to MID and includes a Communications and Records routing page dated September 23.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Peiping Despatch No. 474 and the Kwantung Army
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes and critically evaluates reports about the Kwantung Army’s autonomy and long-term plans.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum outlines the thesis that the Kwantung Army dominated Manchukuo, possessed considerable independence from Tokyo, and sought financial and recruiting autonomy through taxation, a permanent garrison, and Japanese immigration. It notes that local funding and recruitment could insulate the army from future liberal control in Japan. The writer questions the claim that the commander was independent of the General Staff and War Ministry and argues that Manchukuo’s limited revenues and small Japanese population made genuine self-sufficiency doubtful.

subfiles.title: The Kwantung Army: Covering Despatch No. 474
subfiles.from: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Embassy, Peiping
subfiles.about: Transmits Mukden despatch no. 264 on the Kwantung Army’s relations with Manchukuo and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Johnson encloses the May 13 report from the American Consulate General at Mukden. He characterizes it as a discussion of trends affecting the Kwantung Army’s position relative to both the Manchukuo Government and Japan.

subfiles.title: The Kwantung Army
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine, American Consul General at Mukden
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Ambassador at Peiping
subfiles.about: Analyzes the Kwantung Army’s control of Manchukuo, its degree of independence from Tokyo, and its plans for financial and military self-sufficiency.
subfiles.summary: Ballantine describes the Kwantung Army’s control of Manchukuo through liaison between its Third Staff Section and the General Affairs Board, while portraying its commander as formally responsible to the Emperor and only loosely constrained by Tokyo. He argues that declining military prestige after the February 26 Incident and Japanese resentment of Manchurian expenditures could threaten the army’s position. Projects intended to reduce that vulnerability included taxing Japanese residents, improving revenue collection and trade, creating a permanent local garrison, and settling large numbers of Japanese households to supply recruits. He concludes that a locally financed and recruited Kwantung Army could resist policy changes in Japan and profoundly alter relations between Manchukuo, the army, and the home forces.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Relation of the Kwantung Army to the South Manchuria Railway Company
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, Dairen
subfiles.about: Points to another file for a despatch on the Kwantung Army’s relationship with the South Manchuria Railway Company.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs the reader to file 894C.77/24. It identifies a June 19, 1936 despatch from Grummon at Dairen concerning the Kwantung Army and the South Manchuria Railway Company.

subfiles.title: Instance of Difference of Viewpoint between the Kwantung Army and Tokyo War Ministry
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Uses the obstruction of a British air attaché’s tour to illustrate local Kwantung Army independence from Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Commander Chappelle obtained written War Ministry permission and an approved itinerary to inspect airports in Manchuria. Local military authorities nevertheless prevented him from visiting the airports at Heiho and Kungchuling and denied him passage on a previously reserved commercial flight from Dairen to Hsinking. Grummon presents the episode as evidence that Kwantung authorities sometimes acted independently of their nominal Tokyo superiors.

subfiles.title: Departmental Summary of Rumored Kwantung Army Reorganization
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes Mukden rumors of changes intended to give Tokyo greater control over Japanese continental forces.
subfiles.summary: The note reports rumors that General Terauchi might replace General Ueda. An alternative version held that the Kwantung Army would lose its separate identity within a continental high command, probably led by Terauchi.

subfiles.title: Change in the Kwantung Army: Covering Despatch
subfiles.from: John Davies, Jr., American Vice Consul at Mukden
subfiles.about: Transmits a confidential report on rumors of a change in the Kwantung Army.
subfiles.summary: Davies encloses a copy of his despatch no. 200, confidential no. 40, sent to the Embassy at Peiping. The enclosed report concerns possible changes in the organization or command of the Kwantung Army.

subfiles.title: Change in the Kwantung Army
subfiles.from: John Davies, Jr., American Vice Consul at Mukden
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Ambassador at Peiping
subfiles.about: Reports competing rumors about the replacement of General Ueda and creation of a unified Japanese continental command.
subfiles.summary: Several sources claimed that General Ueda would return to Japan and be replaced as Kwantung Army commander by General Terauchi, though Shoichi Kanki denied knowledge of such a move. Another official said instead that the Kwantung Army might be partitioned and absorbed into a high command over all Japanese forces in China and Manchukuo, probably headed by Terauchi. All versions attributed the proposed change to a desire for stronger Tokyo War Office control over forces on the continent.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference to Telegram on Military-Training Films
subfiles.from: Department of State records staff
subfiles.about: Points to the films file for Linnell’s telegram about training films requested by Kwangtung authorities.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers the reader to file 102.Films/165 for Linnell’s July 19 telegram from Canton. It identifies the subject as films for recruit education and asks whether they could be loaned or rented to the Kwangtung authorities.

subfiles.title: Telegram Requesting Military-Training Films for Kwangtung Recruits
subfiles.from: Linnell, Canton
subfiles.about: Requests information about obtaining films on modern military operations and equipment for Kwangtung recruit training.
subfiles.summary: The Kwangtung Governor’s office asked for moving pictures to educate recruits of the Citizens Military Training Department. Requested subjects included aircraft operations, air-defense equipment, guns, fortifications, tanks, poison gas, bridge repair, temporary bridges, and military communications. Linnell asks whether suitable films could properly be loaned or rented to the provincial authorities.
